scientificFoundations.title: Scientific Foundations
scientificFoundations.description: Before conducting research, psychologists rely on a scientific approach grounded in curiosity, skepticism, and humility.

scientificAttitude.name: Scientific Attitude
scientificAttitude.description: The mindset required for good science: curiosity (asking questions), skepticism (questioning claims), humility (being open to being wrong), and an empirical approach (relying on evidence).

scientificMethod.name: Scientific Method
scientificMethod.description: The process of developing and testing ideas: observation → theory (explanation based on observations) → hypothesis (testable prediction) → operational definition (how variables are measured) → testing → replication.
scientificMethod.key: A good hypothesis must be falsifiable — it must be possible to disprove it through observation or experiment.

peerReview.name: Peer Review
peerReview.description: Scientific experts evaluate a research article's theory, originality, methods, and accuracy before publication. This helps ensure findings are credible and valid.

thinkingTraps.name: Hindsight Bias
thinkingTraps.description: The tendency to believe, after an outcome is known, that we 'knew it all along.' No matter the outcome, we convince ourselves it was predictable.
thinkingTraps.example: After a breakup: 'I knew long distance wouldn't work — out of sight, out of mind.' But if they stayed together: 'I knew they'd make it — absence makes the heart grow fonder.'

thinkingTraps.name: Overconfidence
thinkingTraps.description: The tendency to overestimate the accuracy of our knowledge and judgments. Combined with hindsight bias, leads us to overestimate our intuition.
thinkingTraps.example: 82% of US drivers believe they are in the top 30% in driving safety.

validity.name: Validity
validity.description: The extent to which a test or experiment measures or predicts what it is supposed to. A valid study actually tests what it claims to test.
types: Construct validity: does it measure the concept it claims to?
Predictive validity: does it predict future outcomes?

reliability.name: Reliability
reliability.description: The consistency of results — a reliable test yields similar results each time it is administered. Achieved through replication and clear operational definitions.
reliability.note: Larger sample size = more reliable results.

experimentalDesign.title: Experimental Research
experimentalDesign.description: The ONLY type of research that can establish cause and effect. The researcher manipulates an independent variable and measures the effect on a dependent variable.

keyComponents.name: Dependent Variable (DV)
keyComponents.description: What the researcher measures to see if it was affected.

keyComponents.name: Confounding Variable
keyComponents.description: Factors other than the IV that could impact the DV.

keyComponents.name: Control Group
keyComponents.description: Does NOT receive the treatment; serves as baseline comparison.

keyComponents.name: Random Assignment
keyComponents.description: Participants randomly placed into groups to ensure equivalence.

keyComponents.name: Operational Definition
keyComponents.description: Specific description of how a variable will be measured.

keyComponents.name: Hypothesis
keyComponents.description: Researcher's prediction about the relationship between variables. Must be falsifiable.

procedures.name: Single-Blind Study
procedures.description: Participants don't know which group they're in, but the researcher does.

procedures.name: Double-Blind Study
procedures.description: Neither participants NOR researchers interacting with them know group assignment. Controls for experimenter bias.

procedures.name: Placebo
procedures.description: Fake treatment given to control group that looks like the real one.

procedures.name: Nocebo
procedures.description: The opposite of placebo — when belief that a treatment will cause harm actually produces negative side effects, even though the treatment is inactive.

measures.name: Quantitative
measures.description: Numerical data, such as Likert scales (rate on numerical scale).

measures.name: Qualitative
measures.description: Non-numerical data, such as structured interviews with open-ended responses.

nonExperimentalMethods.title: Non-Experimental Research
nonExperimentalMethods.description: Used when it's not possible or ethical to manipulate variables. CANNOT establish cause and effect.

methods.name: Case Study
methods.description: In-depth investigation of a single individual or group.
methods.limitation: Findings may not be generalizable to the broader population.

methods.name: Correlational Research
methods.description: Examines the relationship between two variables without manipulating either one.
methods.strength: Identifies relationships between variables; useful when experiments aren't possible.
methods.limitation: Correlation does NOT equal causation. Cannot determine which variable causes the change. Third variable problem.

methods.name: Meta-Analysis
methods.description: Statistical technique combining results of multiple studies on the same topic.
methods.strength: Provides stronger conclusions by aggregating data across many studies.
methods.limitation: Quality depends on the studies included; can be biased by publication bias.

methods.name: Naturalistic Observation
methods.description: Observing behaviors in their natural setting without interfering.
methods.strength: Captures genuine behavior in real-world contexts.
methods.limitation: Observer may influence behavior (Hawthorne effect); hard to replicate; no control over variables.

methods.name: Survey
methods.description: A research method that collects data by asking many people the same set of questions, either through questionnaires or interviews.
methods.strength: Can gather large amounts of data quickly and cheaply from many participants.
methods.limitation: Responses may not be truthful (social desirability bias), low response rates, and wording effects can drastically change results.

additionalConcepts.name: Wording Effects (Anchoring)
additionalConcepts.description: How a question is worded can drastically change the response. Leading questions, loaded language, or anchoring with a number can skew survey results.
additionalConcepts.example: Asking 'Is the population greater than 10 million?' anchors the estimate higher than asking 'Is the population greater than 1 million?'

additionalConcepts.name: Hawthorne Effect
additionalConcepts.description: When people change their behavior because they know they are being observed, regardless of what is being studied.
additionalConcepts.example: Workers at a factory improved productivity simply because they knew researchers were watching them, not because of any change in working conditions.

additionalConcepts.name: Illusory Correlation
additionalConcepts.description: Perceiving a relationship between two variables when no actual relationship exists. A random coincidence is mistaken for a meaningful connection.
additionalConcepts.example: Believing that starting an adoption process causes pregnancy. To test this, you'd also need to look at cases where people started adoption and did NOT become pregnant.
additionalConcepts.relatedTo: Confirmation bias — we notice confirming cases and ignore disconfirming ones.

correlationDetails.positive: Both variables move in the same direction (e.g., +0.85).
correlationDetails.thirdVariableProblem: An observed correlation between two variables might actually be caused by a third unmeasured variable influencing both.

sampling.title: Sampling Methods
sampling.description: How researchers select participants for their study.

terms.sample: The group of people who actually participate in the study.
terms.population: The larger group from which the sample is drawn.

methods.name: Random Sampling
methods.description: Every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.

methods.name: Convenience Sampling
methods.description: Participants chosen because they are easy to access.
methods.example: Picking students from your own school.
methods.weakness: May not represent the population; introduces sampling bias.

criticalDistinction.randomSampling: How you SELECT participants from a population.
criticalDistinction.randomAssignment: How you PLACE participants into groups once they're in the study.
criticalDistinction.warning: AP exam frequently tests the difference between these two concepts.

sampling.samplingBias: Occurs when the process of selecting the sample is flawed, making certain members more likely to be selected than others.
sampling.generalizability: If your sample does not represent the population, you cannot generalize findings to the broader population.

ethics.title: Research Ethics

guidelines.name: Institutional Review
guidelines.description: Ethics board reviews study before it's conducted to ensure it meets ethical standards. Required for research involving humans and non-human animals.

guidelines.name: Informed Consent
guidelines.description: Participants must be told about the study and agree to participate.

guidelines.name: Informed Assent
guidelines.description: Required when working with minors. Different from informed consent — do not mix them up.

guidelines.name: Protection from Harm
guidelines.description: Researchers must take steps to protect participants from physical and psychological harm.

guidelines.name: Confidentiality
guidelines.description: Participant information must be kept confidential and in some cases anonymous.

guidelines.name: Debriefing
guidelines.description: If deception is used, researchers must explain the true purpose and address concerns afterward.

ethics.deception: Sometimes used in studies; may involve confederates (people pretending to be participants).
ethics.scientificProcess: Experiments and research that can be replicated and go through peer review ensure findings are reliable and valid.

biases.name: Hindsight Bias
biases.description: The 'I-knew-it-all-along' phenomenon — the tendency to believe, after learning an outcome, that we would have predicted it. Makes us overconfident in our ability to predict events.

biases.name: Overconfidence
biases.description: The tendency to overestimate the accuracy of our knowledge and judgments. Combined with hindsight bias, leads us to overestimate our intuition.

biases.name: Experimenter Bias
biases.description: When researcher expectations influence the results.

biases.name: Confirmation Bias
biases.description: Tendency to seek information confirming existing beliefs while ignoring contradicting evidence.

biases.name: Sampling Bias
biases.description: When the sample does not accurately represent the population.

biases.name: Social Desirability Bias
biases.description: Participants respond in ways they think are socially acceptable rather than truthfully.

biases.name: Observer Bias
biases.description: Observer's expectations influence their interpretation of data.

biases.name: Illusory Correlation
biases.description: Perceiving a relationship between two variables when none exists, often due to confirmation bias or memorable coincidences.

scenarios.title: Caffeine and Memory
scenarios.description: A researcher wants to know whether caffeine affects memory performance.
scenarios.confound: If groups study in different environments, noise level is a confound

scenarios.title: Screen Time and Sleep
scenarios.description: Researchers survey 500 teenagers about their daily screen time and sleep quality.
scenarios.warning: Cannot conclude screen time CAUSES poor sleep. A third variable (stress) could influence both.

scenarios.title: Phineas Gage
scenarios.description: An in-depth study of a railroad worker who survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe, causing dramatic personality changes.
scenarios.strength: Provided detailed information about frontal lobe function.
scenarios.limitation: Findings from one individual cannot be generalized to the broader population.
